title: Silent movie theaters and the Fern Dance Hall
summary: Hug played silent movies, then the Fern Dance Hall with Harry Shields, learning to play without music.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Back to the piano players, are there any others that you remember in that era that were outstanding?

Well, I would say that after I began playing around the suburban movie houses in town, I used to play for silent movies in those days. Played with three pieces. We used to get a dollar a piece a night. We didn't even get our call fair, but I was playing with a violin player by the name of Grasshoff and a drummer, Surpass I believe was his name. We used to go down to the St. Maurice Avenue Theater and play for these silent movies. The silent movies got a bad deal in those days because we were playing Tiger Rag or some other rag and there would be a love scene. In other words, it didn't make any difference what was going on. We were just playing the same type of music, but nobody said anything. So from there, I graduated to the Foyne Dance Hall. Well, that was really a real good deal there because I met Harry Shields, he was playing there at the time. Buzzy Willards, a very good banjo player. It's too bad that you couldn't have gotten him down. He played a nice banjo. And Von Gammon was playing drums. Bill Gillen was playing trumpet. I can't remember. I don't believe we had a trombone. No, I don't think we had a trombone. One reed? Only one reed? I believe so. I think we had just Harry Shields on the clarinet. I don't believe we had a trombone player. A bass player? Can't even remember a bass player. Because you know in those days they kept things down to the bone too, you know. Oh yeah. So they probably didn't have a bass player. But that was a great spot in those days. That was about 1926. And it was a great meeting place for all musicians. And of course, they played five hours without taking a break. There was no such thing as stopping. You had to grab a Coca-Cola and play with one hand and ready to sandwich with the other hand, you know. Well, let's see. We played four tunes. I believe we played what was called a slow drag. Well, that was the feature dance of every set. When the announcer would say, get your tickets for the four-minute slow drag, all the customers would gang up for that slow drag. Because that was a slow, that was a long dance, you know. They got their money's worth. And we did a sort of a fast tune and a medium tune. And then we did a waltz. Well, on the waltz, the piano player kept playing. But the balloon instruments would get a little, would get a little rest and the waltz would last about two or three minutes, I guess. So that was the extent of their break. Then we went right back over and started playing, playing the fast tunes again. So everybody would always be looking to see somebody come into place, you know. If it was a piano player or a trumpet player or a clarinet player. They'd get them, come on up. Give me a, sit in. Give me a break. So really we had some of the finest men in the business that would stop in there in those days. Like Shawty used to stop in. Eddie Miller would come in. Fazzola would come in. Oh, just can't think of all the guys. They'd all stop in some time or another. He asked me about piano players. There was a piano player by the name of Von Heck that used to play in those days. I don't know what happened to him. He was a pretty good, pretty good man. And there was another piano player by the name of Ernest Baubach that played piano in those days. I followed him in there, I think. Ernest Baubach? Ernest Baubach or Baubach. I'm not sure as to the exact pronunciation now. And they had of course this piano player by the name of Bill Voorhees. He used to play there. He was a good man. Well, I stayed at the firm for about six months or a year. And I say that I got a good foundation there. Because when I came on the job, I had a few tunes rolled up, you know, a few of the jazz tunes written out, you know. And Von Gammon says, oh, what are you doing with that? He says, you're not going to use any music here. He says, besides it's too dark. He says, you'll never be able to read it. I said, well, how am I going to play? He says, well, we'll show you. Well, I think that's an interesting point there, Dick, to bring out, is how jazz was really started in those days. Because the old timers didn't believe in any music. If you had music on the job, you were a square, strictly a square. You better leave that music home. And Harry Shields was sitting right alongside of me. And I said, how am I going to play this tune, Harry? I never heard of it. I think it was That's A Plenty or Clarinet Long Way or something. Harry says, don't worry about it. He says, you'll learn the chords. Well, boy, I really, on the first couple of times, I must have really hit some dillies. Because Harry gave me some real mean looks, you know. So, I was kind of a little disturbed about it. In fact, Harry kind of made me a little peeve there for a while because he was kind of getting on to me, you know, about the chords I was using. But really, it was really a great thing that he did because, I appreciate it because he taught me the right chords, showed me what I should play. And when I got finished there, I knew most of the old tunes.
